C005.subject: Social features in fasting apps that incorporate real-time accountability partners
C005.object: adherence drop-off rates during the first 30 days of use compared to features focused only on peer encouragement or leaderboards
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Social features in fasting apps that incorporate real-time accountability partners adherence drop-off rates during the first 30 days of use compared to features focused only on peer encouragement or leaderboards]

[PATH:empirical] A randomized controlled trial comparing an intermittent fasting app with real-time accountability partners versus one with peer encouragement/leaderboards only, measuring daily adherence and drop-off rates over 30 days — Direct causal evidence from a controlled experiment would isolate the effect of real-time accountability on adherence, providing the strongest test of the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of health app engagement studies examining the impact of synchronous vs. asynchronous social features on user retention in the first month — Synthesizing existing findings across similar domains (e.g., weight loss, exercise apps) can reveal whether real-time accountability consistently outperforms encouragement-only features, informing the hypothesis without new data collection.

qualifier.geographic: global, primarily in regions with high smartphone penetration and health app adoption

C006.subject: Social features in fasting apps
C006.object: superficial connections that do not translate into long-term adherence or improved well-being for intermittent fasters
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Social features in fasting apps superficial connections that do not translate into long-term adherence or improved well-being for intermittent fasters]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal randomized controlled trial comparing fasting apps with social features vs. without, measuring adherence at 6 and 12 months and well-being outcomes (e.g., psychological distress, social connectedness). — Directly tests whether social features lead to sustained behavior change and improved well-being, addressing the causal claim of superficiality and lack of long-term impact.

[PATH:empirical] Qualitative study using in-depth interviews or diary methods with intermittent fasters using social features, focusing on perceived depth of connections, motivation trajectories, and perceived well-being changes. — Provides rich contextual data on user experiences, revealing whether connections are superficial and how they influence adherence and well-being over time.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of gamification and social features in digital health interventions, specifically for dietary behavior change, examining effect sizes for long-term adherence and psychological outcomes. — Synthesizes existing evidence across similar domains to assess generalizability of the claim that social features in health apps produce only superficial effects.

C007.subject: Social features in fasting apps that incorporate real-time group challenges and shared progress dashboards
C007.object: significant improvements in both adherence and self-reported well-being for intermittent fasters compared to apps with only passive social feeds
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Social features in fasting apps that incorporate real-time group challenges and shared progress dashboards significant improvements in both adherence and self-reported well-being for intermittent fasters compared to apps with only passive social feeds]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing a fasting app with real-time group challenges and shared dashboards versus one with only passive social feeds, measuring adherence (e.g., fasting logs) and well-being (e.g., WHO-5 or PANAS) over 12 weeks in urban high-income populations. — Directly tests the causal claim with high internal validity; addresses the specific comparator and outcomes.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of social features in digital health interventions for behavior change (e.g., gamification, social accountability) in dietary adherence contexts. — Provides broader evidence on whether real-time interactive social features outperform passive feeds, and identifies effect sizes and moderators relevant to intermittent fasting.

[PATH:empirical] Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study within an existing fasting app user base, comparing adherence and well-being trajectories between users who opt into group challenges vs. those who use only passive feeds, controlling for self-selection via propensity score matching. — Offers real-world evidence with high external validity; can capture temporal dynamics and user engagement patterns over 12 weeks.

qualifier.geographic: in urban populations in high-income countries

C008.subject: Social features in fasting apps
C008.object: adherence and well-being for intermittent fasters through meaningful community support
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Social features in fasting apps adherence and well-being for intermittent fasters through meaningful community support]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing fasting app usage with vs. without social features, measuring adherence (e.g., fasting logs) and well-being (e.g., validated scales like WHO-5) over 12 weeks — Directly tests causal effect of social features on outcomes under controlled conditions, reducing confounding from self-selection bias.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of digital health interventions for dietary adherence, focusing on community support mechanisms (e.g., forums, leaderboards, peer messaging) — Synthesizes existing evidence across multiple studies to assess whether community features consistently improve adherence and well-being, and identifies moderators (e.g., app design, user demographics).

[PATH:empirical] Qualitative study using in-depth interviews or focus groups with intermittent fasters who use fasting apps with social features, exploring perceived mechanisms of community support (e.g., accountability, shared experience, emotional validation) — Provides explanatory insight into how and why social features might enhance or hinder adherence and well-being, informing theoretical refinement and hypothesis generation.

C011.subject: Streak-based social features in fasting apps
C011.predicate: increase user dropout rates after 30 days
C011.object: by creating a binary success/failure mindset that punishes brief lapses
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Streak-based social features in fasting apps by creating a binary success/failure mindset that punishes brief lapses]

[PATH:empirical] A longitudinal randomized controlled trial comparing fasting apps with and without streak-based social features, measuring user retention and dropout at 30, 60, and 90 days. — Directly tests causal effect of streak features on dropout, controlling for other app elements, and captures temporal dynamics beyond 30 days.

[PATH:empirical] Qualitative interview study with users who have dropped out of fasting apps, focusing on their experiences with streak mechanics and perceived failure. — Provides rich data on the psychological mechanism (binary success/failure mindset) hypothesized to mediate dropout, which quantitative metrics alone cannot capture.

[PATH:theoretical] Review of self-determination theory literature on goal-contingent rewards and all-or-nothing thinking in health behavior change (e.g., work by Ryan & Deci, or studies on 'what the hell' effect in dieting). — Anchors the hypothesis in established theory, allowing evaluation of whether streak features likely undermine intrinsic motivation and trigger ego-depletion or shame cycles, as predicted.
